answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a way of measuring directed information flow between two elements — here, two neurons — rather than just their similarity. Where mutual information (introduced just before this in the same passage) tells you how much two neurons' activity patterns resemble each other, without any sense of which one is influencing which, transfer entropy asks a more specific question: does knowing the past activity of neuron X help predict the future activity of neuron Y, over and above what Y's own past already tells you about itself?

The article defines this properly a little further on: transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on the target's own past, and is read as the transfer entropy from the source's past to the target's future. The conditioning on Y's own past matters — it's what stops the measure from just picking up each neuron's tendency to keep doing what it was already doing (autocorrelation), and isolates the genuine contribution of X.

This distinction matters for the sentence you selected because it sets up the two main tools of section 2: mutual information and transfer entropy are well suited to this purpose of tracking how information propagates through a neural system. The article goes on to frame this as a difference in kind, not just degree: mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, whereas transfer entropy measures effective connectivity — meaning mutual information just flags a statistical association, while transfer entropy makes a claim about directional influence. This groundwork matters because the rest of the paper builds toward partial information decomposition, which needs exactly this notion of directed, time-ordered dependence between source neurons and a target to ask how those sources' signals combine or interact, rather than merely how correlated they are.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This sentence names the two specific statistical tools the article is about to unpack, and both get spelled out in the paragraphs right after this one.

Mutual information measures whether knowing the activity of one neuron tells you anything about another neuron's activity — it can be thought of as a nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity. The article stresses that this is not directional: it does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow."

Transfer entropy is the tool that adds that missing sense of direction and time. Transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on the target's own past. In other words, it asks: once you already know a neuron's own recent history, does knowing another neuron's history let you predict its next move any better? The article summarizes the contrast this way: Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity.

So the sentence you selected is essentially a signpost: it tells you that to "track" information moving through a neural circuit — the topic of this section — these are the two workhorse measures, one for undirected statistical dependence (mutual information) and one for directed, predictive information flow (transfer entropy). Both are set up here as stepping stones toward the paper's real focus later on: partial information decomposition, which goes beyond tracking flow between pairs to ask how multiple inputs are combined or "processed" by a target neuron.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this article, transfer entropy is a way of measuring directed information flow between two neurons over time — specifically, how much knowing the past activity of one neuron (the source) reduces uncertainty about the future activity of another neuron (the target), after you've already accounted for what the target's own past tells you about itself [spya-p4pyuy]. The article gives the formal definition, and notes that the source's "past" doesn't have to be a single time bin — it can be a more complex, multi-dimensional window [spya-p4pyuy]. It contrasts this with plain mutual information, which is undirected and doesn't capture "flow": mutual information is described as a measure of functional connectivity, while transfer entropy measures effective connectivity — actual information propagation [spya-p4pyuy].

Why it matters to the argument: the piece uses transfer entropy as the tool that first lets researchers map out an "effective network" of directed influence among recorded neurons — which pairs are meaningfully sending information to which others [spya-sw5ukx]. But the article is explicit that this measure of flow, however useful, has a ceiling: it can't show how multiple streams of information are combined or transformed into something new. As it puts it, information transfer captures overall "flow" but is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information "interact" and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources [spya-s0db2g]. That gap is exactly the motivation for bringing in partial information decomposition (PID): transfer entropy tells you how much a source's past informs a target's future, but not how two sources' pasts jointly inform it in a way irreducible to either alone — which is what PID is built to isolate as "synergy" [spya-wer4cd, spya-u5ra3d].

So structurally, transfer entropy sets up the problem the rest of the article solves: it's the tool that identifies which connections in a circuit carry information, and its very limitation — no notion of joint, higher-order interaction — is the reason the authors turn to PID as the more powerful successor method. Later empirical sections keep transfer entropy in play as a companion measure (e.g., testing whether synergy tracks the amount of transfer entropy in a triad) [spya-kqkb58], so it never disappears — it's the baseline against which PID's added insight is measured.

Synergistic is the key technical term this whole review is built around, and it names one of the three modes into which the paper's central tool—partial information decomposition (PID)—splits the information that a set of neurons carries about a target.

The idea is this: if you have two source neurons feeding into a target, you can ask how much each source alone tells you about the target's future state, and how much the two sources tell you together. Ordinarily you might expect the "together" amount to just be the sum of the two "alone" amounts. But it often isn't. When the joint information is *greater* than the sum of the individual contributions, that surplus is called synergy — "there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In this case, the system exhibits synergistic dynamics." The opposite case, where the sources overlap and duplicate each other, is called redundancy.

The reason the abstract singles out synergy as the mode worth focusing on is that it's the piece that looks like genuine computation rather than mere information relay: "PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources. We focus particularly on the synergistic mode, which quantifies the 'higher-order' information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source." Later in the paper the authors elaborate that a target neuron showing synergy "can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating 'computation' on all of its inputs considered jointly" — it's not just adding up signals, it's reading the pattern across them.

The abstract also previews where synergy shows up empirically: "synergistic dynamics are ubiquitous in neural circuitry and show reliable structure–function relationships, emerging disproportionately in neuronal rich clubs, downstream of recurrent connectivity, and in the convergence of correlated activity." Those findings are worked out in detail later in the article (the rich-club, recurrent-connection, and correlated-input sections), so this word here in the abstract is essentially flagging the paper's main finding before the machinery behind it—mutual information, transfer entropy, and finally the PID framework itself—has been introduced.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This is naming the three-way split that partial information decomposition (PID) produces, and it's worth unpacking each term since the rest of the article builds on exactly this vocabulary.

When a target neuron's activity depends on two or more source neurons, the total information those sources carry about the target can be broken into pieces that don't overlap. Redundant information is the part that any of the sources could tell you on its own — it's duplicated, so you don't gain anything from having more than one source report it. Unique information is the part only one particular source can tell you, something the others don't carry at all. Synergistic information is the interesting case: it only shows up when you look at the sources' joint pattern together, and vanishes if you look at each source in isolation — it's the extra information created by the combination itself, not present in any single input.

The abstract flags synergy as the one the paper cares about most, describing it as "the “higher-order” information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source." That's because synergy is treated as the signature of actual computation or integration by the target neuron, rather than just passive relaying of a single upstream signal — a distinction the article later formalizes with the two-source neuron example, where the target's decision to fire depends on the joint pattern of its inputs, not their sum.

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" here refers to the portion of information about a target neuron's future activity that can only be learned by observing two or more source neurons jointly — it disappears if you look at either source alone. The article defines this formally through the equation comparing joint mutual information to the sum of individual (marginal) mutual information terms: if the whole is greater than the sum of the parts, that surplus is synergistic information, and the target neuron is performing "a kind of integrating 'computation'" on its inputs considered jointly [spya-e94ury]. Figure 1's description frames it as the space left over once you subtract what each source independently and redundantly accounts for from the total information the sources jointly carry about the target [spya-pjdgu6].

Synergy matters to the argument because the whole piece is trying to locate "information processing" itself, not just information transfer. The authors are explicit that measuring flow (via mutual information or transfer entropy) tells you the system is passing signals around, but not whether it is doing anything to those signals — it "is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information 'interact' and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources" [spya-s0db2g]. Synergy is proposed as the marker that fills that gap: it captures information "not reducible to input from any single source," which the abstract treats as the quantitative signature of higher-order computation [spya-xn9j9k].

The empirical sections then build the whole case for synergy's importance on this foundation: synergy is shown to concentrate disproportionately in richly-connected "rich club" neurons, to increase with recurrent connectivity, and to depend on how correlated converging inputs are [spya-fud8q3 spya-sd9fzd spya-hkhpex]. In the summary, the authors tie this back to their central claim explicitly: the existence of synergy shows that "neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total... but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli" [spya-rc5z33]. So synergy is the concept that lets the article argue neurons are genuine computational elements — combining, not just relaying, their inputs — rather than simple summation devices.
